strengths: Clear problem formulation with explicit requirements (R1-R4) and systematic analysis of prior work limitations in Table 1
Novel adapter merging approach using spectral norm clipping to address over-refusal when combining multiple feature-locking adapters
Comprehensive experimental evaluation across multiple attack types (naive, non-adaptive, adaptive jailbreaks) and feature combinations (2-4 simultaneous locks)
Genuine scalability improvement: trains one adapter per feature rather than requiring exponential adapters for feature combinations (2^N-1 with alternative approaches)
Strong empirical results with near-perfect effectiveness (0.00 utility on locked features) and acceptable utility preservation (mostly ≤3% degradation, max 7%)
Substantial improvements over password-locking baseline (e.g., 95%→5% attack success rate reduction on AutoDAN for Math)
Responsible disclosure of limitations including feature interference, model diversity constraints, and computational costs
weaknesses: Limited architectural diversity: only 3 models tested (2 DeepSeek variants + 1 Llama), all 7-8B parameters, no evaluation on larger models or different architecture families (Mistral, GPT variants), limiting generalization claims

Hyperparameter sensitivity undermines scalability claims: τ parameter requires different values for each feature combination (16+ values for one model), no principled method for setting τ for new combinations, contradicting the claimed scalability advantage

Feature interference inadequately addressed: acknowledged 6% utility drop when locking U on Llama (Table 2) and M-U interactions, but investigation relegated to future work despite being critical for multi-feature scenarios

Robustness evaluation has limitations: ASR metric is crude and gameable, attacks use only 1,000 samples, temperature fixed at 0, no evaluation of adaptive attacks specifically designed against LOCKET (only adapted standard jailbreaks)
Incomplete baseline comparisons: only compares against one baseline (password-locking), dismisses alternative approaches (system prompts, classifiers, multiple LLMs) without empirical evaluation

Incremental core novelty: combines well-established techniques (LoRA adapters, KL-divergence utility preservation, Latent Adversarial Training) with spectral norm clipping as the primary novel component

Feature definition ambiguity: uses synthetic feature groupings with unclear operational separation in practice; assumes non-overlapping features despite observed M-U interference suggesting features may be entangled
Theoretical justification limited: why spectral norm clipping specifically prevents over-refusal is intuitive but not rigorously justified; no bounds on utility degradation given clipping threshold

strengths: Clear and comprehensive problem formulation with well-defined requirements (R1-R4) that enable systematic evaluation
Thorough empirical evaluation against multiple state-of-the-art jailbreak attacks (Many-shot, GCG, TAP, AutoDAN) across three models
Practical technical contribution addressing over-refusal through spectral norm clipping in adapter merging
Honest acknowledgment of limitations (feature interference, model scope, computational costs)
Effective use of requirement framework (Table 1) to compare with prior work
weaknesses: Limited research novelty: Core contributions are straightforward applications of existing techniques (LoRA + LAT + standard adapter merging); spectral norm clipping is a simple heuristic without theoretical justification
Questionable problem motivation: API-level authentication is a simpler, more secure, standard solution already deployed by providers; embedding feature-locking in models is artificial

Overstated scalability claims: Each feature combination requires separate τ tuning (Appendix B shows many different values), contradicting efficiency claims; only empirically validated to 4 features with speculative claims about 12

Fundamental feature separation issues: Paper reports up to 6% utility drops due to feature interference (Table 2), undermining the premise of cleanly lockable independent features; feature definitions appear ad-hoc
Evaluation gaps: Only tested against four attack types; no adaptive attacks assuming attacker knows LOCKET mechanism; robustness claims presented too confidently given rapid jailbreak evolution
Weak baseline comparison: Only one baseline (PWD); no comparison with practical alternatives (API routing, multiple models); PWD and LOCKET evaluated under different threat models
Hyperparameter sensitivity: τ requires careful tuning (Figure 2) and uses only 100 random examples for validation—stability and generalization unclear; suggests the method is brittle
Misalignment with ACL: Paper is primarily systems/engineering work about model deployment, not NLP research; limited ML/NLP contributions beyond combining existing techniques
Artificial threat model: Assumes service providers deploy models with access to unlocked features clients can exploit, which doesn't reflect real-world practice

Over-refusal problem indicates fundamental issues: The need for specialized merging suggests the base training produces crude refusal behavior ('Sorry, sorry, sorry...'), implying the approach has deeper problems

strengths: Well-motivated and clearly formulated problem with systematic requirements (R1-R4) that clearly articulate why prior password-locking methods are insufficient
Comprehensive experimental evaluation across multiple models, features, feature combinations, and strong jailbreak attacks with detailed comparisons to prior work
Strong empirical results meeting all four requirements (100% effectiveness, ≤7% utility loss, ≤5% attack success, scalability to 4 features) with clear improvements over password-locking baselines
Practical design eliminates credential vulnerabilities (R3.4) that plague password-based approaches, preventing credential theft and unauthorized sharing
Honest treatment of limitations and comprehensive reporting of implementation details, datasets, and hyperparameters supporting reproducibility and code release commitment
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: primarily combines existing techniques (LoRA, LAT from concurrent work, established merging methods) with spectral norm clipping as the main contribution—a relatively incremental methodological advance
Spectral norm clipping approach lacks theoretical justification or ablations; no comparison with alternative metrics (Frobenius norm, other matrix properties); appears ad-hoc despite effectiveness
Methodologically concerning hyperparameter tuning on test set (100 examples per feature for τ); different τ per feature combination contradicts scalability claims and risks overfitting

Feature interference only briefly addressed despite 6% utility drops observed; acknowledged as unsolved ('only in a few cases') with no principled mitigation strategy despite being critical for real deployments

Scalability claims exceed empirical validation: only 4 features tested despite claims of scaling to 12+; relies on citation to prior work rather than own experiments; hyperparameter tuning per combination suggests limited generalization

Attack evaluation gaps: adaptive jailbreaks (R3.3) tested only on single-feature models with transferability assumed but not verified for multi-feature cases; no evaluation of zero-shot or few-shot attack vectors; perturbation budget ε underspecified

Practical deployment concerns unaddressed: feature definition in real systems unclear; client authentication mechanism not discussed; no analysis of handling feature drift, model updates, or trial access

Computational overhead not analyzed: inference latency from spectral decomposition and clipping not measured; per-adapter training cost not reported; suggests hardware-level optimizations needed but not explored

strengths: Well-motivated problem with clear requirements framework (R1-R4) that systematically shows prior work limitations
Novel spectral norm-based merging approach that addresses the over-refusal problem when combining adapters
Comprehensive evaluation across multiple models, datasets, and state-of-the-art adversarial attacks with strong empirical results (100% refusal, ≤7% utility drop, ≤5% ASR)
Thorough experimental methodology with good ablations, scalability testing up to 8 features, and validation on larger models (Llama-3-70B)
Clear presentation with well-structured problem formulation, detailed implementation details for reproducibility, and promise to open-source
weaknesses: Scalability limitations undermine R4 claims: Table 9 shows ineffective locking (orange cells) with 6+ features, contradicting the R4 requirement; feature interference remains unresolved
Core technical contribution lacks theoretical justification: no principled explanation for why spectral norm clipping prevents over-refusal or why τ∈[0,1] is appropriate
Significant hyperparameter tuning overhead: different τ values required for each feature combination and model (15+ values in Appendix E), limiting generalization and practical applicability
Limited baseline comparisons: only systematic evaluation against PWD; strawman techniques discussed but not empirically evaluated; no comparison with other regularization approaches
Credential sharing protection (R3.4) is overstated: method only prevents extracting passwords from weights, not account/feature sharing; users can still share accounts
Feature interference between overlapping features (Math-MMLU) causes up to 6% utility degradation with no practical solution provided; features must be carefully decomposed

Robustness evaluation limitations: ASR based on refusal keywords that could be circumvented; adversary model assumes unrealistic white-box access; temperature=0 evaluation may not reflect real sampling
Limited model coverage: mainly 7B-8B models; Llama-3-70B only in appendix; no evaluation on closed-source models or very large scales
Narrow problem scope: only task-based feature locking; applicability to fine-grained or content-based locking unexplored; features must be task-level categories
Business model assumptions unvalidated: no evidence users accept per-feature pricing; fairness implications and comparison with tiered subscription profitability not discussed

strengths: Well-motivated and clearly formulated problem with systematic comparison of prior work against defined requirements (R1-R4)
Novel spectral norm-clipping approach for adapter merging that effectively mitigates over-refusal when combining multiple feature-locking adapters
Comprehensive experimental evaluation across multiple models, adversarial attacks, and metrics with detailed results tables
Strong core empirical results on effectiveness (100% refusal) and robustness (≤5% attack success rates) for the 4-feature setting
Technically sound and reproducible methodology with detailed hyperparameters and ablations in appendices
weaknesses: Practical motivation is questionable: the claim that pay-to-unlock features is more economical than tiered models lacks LLM-specific evidence and relies on analogy to different domains (software, mobile games)
Feature interference is significant and inadequately addressed: locking Math zeros MMLU performance (0.00 vs 0.53) and vice versa, fundamentally violating the utility-preservation requirement (R2)

Scalability claims are overstated: while claiming to support multiple features, the method degrades significantly at 6+ features (Table 9 shows orange cells for ineffective locking) and admits ~15% utility loss at 8 features, limiting practical deployment

Threat model has critical gaps: no evaluation of white-box attacks on adapter weights, no analysis of fine-tuning attacks on local copies, insufficient discussion of extraction attacks, and claim of R3.4 protection oversimplifies credential sharing risks

Hyperparameter sensitivity undermines scalability: the scaling parameter τ requires different values (0.45-0.9) per feature combination with no principled selection method for new features, requiring tuning on held-out test data

Limited technical novelty: primarily combines existing techniques (LoRA, LAT, preference learning) with one relatively simple innovation (spectral norm clipping); lacks ablation showing how much robustness comes from LAT vs the merging approach

Evaluation methodology concerns: greedy decoding (temperature=0) for main results with limited stochastic validation; weak baseline (password-locking not designed for utility); attack success metrics based only on refusal keyword presence are simplistic

Questionable venue fit: this is a systems/security paper with limited relevance to core NLP/computational linguistics research; methods are applications of existing techniques to a niche practical problem
Significant scalability ceiling acknowledged but inadequately emphasized: practical real-world scenarios with many premium features would exceed the 8-10 adapter merging limit the paper demonstrates

strengths: Well-motivated problem with clear requirement specification (R1-R4) systematically compared against prior work
Novel spectral-norm-based adapter merging approach that effectively prevents over-refusal, a key insight missing in prior merging methods

Comprehensive experimental evaluation across multiple models (7B, 8B, 70B), four features, and four different adversarial attack types with strong empirical results (100% refusal, ≤7% utility loss, ≤5% ASR)
Practical low-overhead system design (1±0.06s adapter attachment, minimal inference latency) with clear real-world applicability for LLM monetization
Thorough reproducibility preparation with detailed hyperparameters, public datasets, implementation details, and promise to open-source
Systematic and fair comparison with strong baseline (password-locking) demonstrating clear improvements across all dimensions
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: primarily combines existing techniques (LoRA, CAT, LAT); spectral norm clipping is a straightforward heuristic without theoretical justification

Feature interference problem inadequately addressed—up to 6% utility drop on overlapping features, and Table 9 shows only 34% effective locking for Philosophy with 8 features locked; proposed mitigation strategies are vague and untested
Scalability claims overstated—while claiming scalability to multiple features, results degrade significantly with 8+ features, and τ requires per-feature-combination tuning

Adversarial robustness evaluation limitations: uses temperature=0 (not reflecting production), only evaluates against current attacks, acknowledges arms race problem, no evaluation of attacks specifically designed against spectral norm clipping
Limited model coverage: main evaluation on smaller models (7-8B); 70B evaluation only in appendix with 4-bit quantization; no evaluation on diverse architectures
Weak economic justification—motivation relies on single anecdotal quote from Sam Altman without market research or financial modeling
Fixed refusal message vulnerability not discussed; no evaluation of prompt engineering attacks targeting the specific refusal format or pattern
Missing ablation studies isolating contributions of LAT vs. spectral norm clipping vs. loss formulation
Limited comparison with recent related work beyond password-locking baselines; no comparison with newer unlearning or selective refusal approaches
